title: Life Together: The One Anothers and the Communal Faith
subtitle: The New Testament knows nothing of a private, solo Christianity. The faith is irreducibly communal, written in roughly fifty-nine commands to do something to one another, love, bear, confess, forgive, spur on, none of which a person can obey alone. What Scripture, church history, and honest research say about the body of Christ, the danger of the just-me-and-Jesus faith, and why you cannot become a disciple by yourself.

parts.title: The Faith You Were Sold and the One the Bible Assumes
parts.body:
You were handed a private faith, and you did not choose it so much as breathe it. Somewhere along the way Christianity became, for you and for nearly everyone around you, a transaction between a soul and its God, a personal relationship with Jesus, a quiet thing kept mostly between the two of you. Church became a service you attend, a building you visit, a place where you sit in rows facing forward, near other people but not actually with them, and then drive home to a life they will never see. You believe. You pray. You read. And you do all of it, fundamentally, alone.

Nobody told you this was a problem. It felt, if anything, like the mature version of faith, the inward kind, the kind that does not need other people getting in the way of you and God. You have heard the slogans your whole life, it is a relationship not a religion, all that matters is your heart, you do not need the church to be a Christian. And so you built a faith you can carry by yourself, portable, independent, requiring no one, and you have never quite noticed that the New Testament does not contain a single example of it.

Here is what should unsettle you. The early Christians could not have understood the question, can I follow Jesus on my own, because the faith they received came as a body, not a private possession. When you actually open the letters of the New Testament, you find they are written almost entirely to communities, in the plural, and they are stuffed with commands you cannot keep by yourself. Love one another. Bear one another's burdens. Confess your sins to one another. Forgive one another. Spur one another on. Roughly fifty-nine times the New Testament tells Christians to do something to one another, and every last one of them requires an other. A solo Christian cannot obey a single one.

Let me say the thing the individualist age trained you not to hear. The private faith you were sold is not a deeper version of Christianity. It is a smaller one, an amputated one, a faith with most of its commands rendered impossible by design. You were made for a body, called into a body, and saved into a body, and the loneliness you have learned to call spiritual maturity is in fact a wound. The good news is that the body is real, it is near, and you can stop trying to follow Jesus by yourself, which you were never able to do anyway.

parts.title: Why a Private Faith Cannot Make a Disciple
parts.body:
The stakes begin with a failure we have stopped noticing because we are swimming in it. The American church largely accepted the terms of the surrounding culture, took the most individualistic society in human history at its word, and rebuilt the faith to fit. We made Christianity a product for the religious consumer, a service to be sampled, an experience tailored to the self, and we wondered why the people kept staying the same. You cannot consume your way into the likeness of Christ. The faith was never a product, and the moment we treated it as one we guaranteed a church full of customers and starved of disciples.

The private faith fails because the very commands of Christ require an other to obey. You cannot practice patience in an empty room. You cannot forgive someone who is not there. You cannot bear a burden that has not been laid against your own. The one-anothers are not optional extras for unusually social Christians. They are the curriculum of sanctification itself, the actual means by which God sands off our selfishness, and they only function inside relationships close enough to chafe. Remove the others, and you have removed the workshop where character is made, and kept only the comfortable illusion that you were growing.

The stakes sharpen in a post-Christian America already drowning in loneliness, where the surgeon general has named isolation a public health emergency and people are starving for exactly the thing the church was built to be. The world cannot supply real belonging, having dismantled the institutions that once carried it, and into that hunger a true Christian community is one of the most powerful witnesses left. Not the program, not the polish, the body, a people who actually share their lives, carry each other's burdens, and love across every line the world keeps. The skeptic who would argue with your doctrine for an hour cannot argue with a community he has never seen anywhere else.

And the stakes are finally about whether discipleship happens at all, because a faith you keep to yourself reproduces nothing. A solo Christian has no one to teach, no one to confess to, no one to be shaped by, no one to send. The chain of faith, which has always run from one life into another, simply ends. But a Christian embedded in a body learns the faith the only way it has ever been learned, by living it out against the friction of real people, and so becomes someone able to pass it on. This is the difference between a faith that survives a generation and one that dies with the person who privatized it. The body is not the setting where discipleship occasionally happens. It is the place where it happens at all.

parts.title: The One Body the New Testament Assumes
parts.body:
Start with the strangest fact about the New Testament, the one familiarity has hidden. Almost none of it was written to individuals. The letters are addressed to churches, to the saints at Philippi, to the church of God in Corinth, to all in Rome, and the you that fills them is, in the original, overwhelmingly plural. When Paul says you are God's temple, he does not mean each of you is a little shrine. He means you together, the whole community, are the place where God dwells. We have spent centuries reading the plural commands of the New Testament as if they were private mail, and in doing so we have quietly unmade the very thing they were written to build.

Then there are the one-anothers, scattered across the letters like the genetic code of the new humanity. Love one another, John records Jesus saying, as I have loved you, and by this everyone will know you are mine. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. Forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you. Encourage one another and build one another up. Spur one another on toward love and good works. Welcome one another. Be kind to one another. Bear with one another. Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Count fifty-nine of them or thereabouts, and notice the single thing they all share. Not one can be obeyed alone. The Christian life, as the New Testament defines it, is a set of mutual actions that presuppose a community, and a faith without others is a faith that cannot do what Jesus commanded.

Go to the picture Paul reached for when he wanted to explain what the church actually is, in the twelfth chapter of First Corinthians. The church is a body, he says, one body with many members, and the members are not interchangeable units but a hand, an eye, a foot, each indispensable, none able to say to the other I have no need of you. This is not a flattering metaphor for a club. It is an account of how God designed his people to be radically dependent, knit so closely that when one suffers all suffer and when one is honored all rejoice. A solitary Christian, in this picture, is not a smaller version of the body. It is a severed limb, alive for a moment, dying by definition, because a hand that has decided it can manage without the body has misunderstood what a hand is for.

Watch the first church actually live this in the second and fourth chapters of Acts. They devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers, and they were together and had all things in common, selling possessions and distributing to any who had need, day by day in the temple and in their homes. They held a community of goods so radical that, Luke says, there was not a needy person among them, because those who had sold lands and houses laid the proceeds at the apostles feet. This was not a commune imposed by law but a love so concrete it touched the property lines. The first thing the Spirit produced at Pentecost was not a feeling. It was a community that shared its bread, its homes, and its money, and the watching city found it irresistible.

And the communal life runs to the foundation of everything, because the God who made us is himself a communion. Before there was a world there was the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, an eternal life of self-giving love, and we are made in that image, which means we are made for one another and not for solitude. It is not good that the man should be alone, God says over the only thing in a finished creation he calls not good. We are saved, then, not into a private relationship but into a people, the household of God, a chosen race, a holy nation, a body fitted together and growing up into Christ. The end of the whole story is not a million separate souls each alone with God. It is a city, a wedding feast, a countless multitude gathered as one, and the communal life you were made for is not a means to that end but a foretaste of it, begun now, in the room down the street where the body meets.

parts.title: How the Church Has Lived Together
parts.body:
The early church astonished the ancient world precisely by how it lived together. Tertullian, writing around the year 197, records the pagans saying of the Christians, see how they love one another, and explains that believers held a common purse, cared for the poor and the orphan and the prisoner, and treated strangers as family. The Roman world had charity for one's own kind and contempt for the rest, and here was a movement that fed widows it had never met and buried the dead of plagues everyone else had fled. The historian who studied the church's growth concluded that this concrete, costly love was a primary engine of its spread. The world was not argued into the faith. It was loved into it, by a community that did in public what the gospel claimed in private.

When the church grew comfortable and the fire dimmed, the communal vision did not die but went looking for harder ground. Antony went to the desert around the year 270, and within a generation thousands had followed, and out of that movement came the monastic communities, men and women who pledged to share everything and to bear with one another for life. When Benedict wrote his Rule in the sixth century, he built it on stability, the vow to stay with this particular flawed community and not to flee to an imagined better one, because he understood that you are formed by the people you cannot leave. The monastery preserved, in concentrated form, the conviction the wider church kept losing, that holiness is made in common life and not in isolation.

The insight kept resurfacing wherever the faith grew warm again. The Moravians under Zinzendorf in the eighteenth century rebuilt a community of shared life so intense it launched the modern missionary movement. John Wesley, shaped by them, made the small group the engine of the Methodist revival, gathering ordinary people into bands and classes where they asked one another the searching question, how is it with your soul, and confessed their sins and watched over one another in love. Wesley said flatly that he knew no holiness but social holiness, by which he did not mean activism but that there is no such thing as a solitary Christian, that the faith is perfected only in company. The revival that reshaped a nation ran, at ground level, on a few people in a room being honest with each other every week.

And then, in 1939, with the German church capitulating to Hitler and his underground seminary at Finkenwalde already shut by the Gestapo, Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a small book called Life Together, and it remains the sharpest word the modern church has on this. Christian community, he insisted, is not an ideal we achieve but a gift we receive, given to us through and in Jesus Christ alone, and the moment we love our dream of community more than the actual people God has given us, we become destroyers of community even as we demand it. He called this the wish-dream, and he warned that the person who enters Christian fellowship demanding it match their fantasy will be perpetually disappointed, accusing the brethren, accusing God, and finally accusing themselves, when all along the disappointment was the necessary death of an idol. Bonhoeffer also recovered what the Protestant world had nearly lost, the practice of confession to one another, arguing that the sin we keep hidden in the solitude of the heart festers, and that to confess it to a brother is to drag it into the light where Christ can kill it. He had earned the right to say it. Within six years he would be hanged for resisting the regime his church had blessed, and the man who wrote that we are saved into community died in a camp, alone in body, and never alone at all.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The social sciences have studied loneliness, belonging, community, and how human beings are shaped by the people around them, and a believer can receive what they have learned gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of why community matters carries a hidden picture of what a person is and what they are for, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.source: The research on loneliness as a public health crisis
secular.author: Vivek Murthy and the surgeon general advisory on isolation
secular.whatItGetsRight: Murthy and a growing field of researchers have established that chronic loneliness is not merely painful but physically lethal, raising the risk of early death on a scale comparable to smoking, and that modern Western life has manufactured isolation at a population level. The work proves with hard data what Scripture asserts on the first pages, that the human being is not built to be alone, and that the absence of real community is a wound to body and soul alike. It names the hunger that the church was built to answer.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research diagnoses the wound and cannot supply the medicine it would take to heal it. It can show that human beings wither in isolation and it cannot produce the kind of community that does not also wither, because the connection it prescribes is grounded in mutual benefit, and mutual benefit dissolves the moment the other person becomes a cost. Scripture grounds Christian community not in what we get from one another but in a prior love that came to us when we were enemies. The science rightly measures the famine. The gospel supplies a bread that does not run out, a belonging held together by Christ and not by how useful we remain to each other.

secular.source: The study of how character is shaped by community
secular.author: Jonathan Haidt and moral-formation research
secular.whatItGetsRight: Haidt and others in moral psychology have shown that human character is not self-generated but caught from the communities we inhabit, that our deepest moral intuitions are formed in groups, and that the modern fiction of the autonomous self choosing its own values in isolation is simply false to how people actually become who they are. This is a sharp confirmation of what the one-anothers assume, that a person is forged by the people they live among, and that you cannot grow a virtue in a vacuum.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research illuminates the mechanism of formation and is silent on its true source and aim. It can tell us that community shapes character and it cannot tell us into whose image we ought to be shaped, treating the group itself as the highest authority when Scripture says a community can form people beautifully into something damned. The one-anothers are not merely social conditioning toward whatever the group prizes. They are the means by which the Spirit conforms us to Christ, who is the standard outside the group that judges and saves it. The science rightly recovers the communal nature of formation. The gospel names the One we are being formed into and the One who does the forming.

secular.author: Robert Bellah and the authors of Habits of the Heart
secular.whatItGetsRight: Bellah and his colleagues, studying American life in the 1980s, named the dominant creed of the modern West as expressive individualism, the conviction that the self is sovereign, that meaning is found by looking inward and being true to oneself, and that all commitments, including religious ones, are finally optional and chosen by the self for the self. Their work explains with precision how Christianity in America became a private, consumer faith, a relationship between a soul and its God with the community treated as elective. It diagnoses exactly the air we breathe.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The diagnosis is acute and the cure it gropes toward, more commitment, thicker community, cannot finally be willed by the very self it has exposed as sovereign. Bellah saw that the autonomous self cannot bind itself for long, and he could not name the only thing that breaks the self's sovereignty, the lordship of Christ who buys us out of self-ownership entirely. Scripture says we are not our own, that we were bought with a price, and only a self that has been dethroned can truly belong to a body. The research rightly names the disease of the sovereign self. The gospel announces the rightful King who alone can heal it by taking the throne the self has usurped.

secular.source: The research on social capital and the collapse of association
secular.author: Robert Putnam and the study of community decline
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented the steady collapse of communal life in modern America, the emptying of the clubs, the churches, the shared tables, the volunteer associations that once bound people together, and showed how much human flourishing depends on the thick webs of belonging he called social capital. His work establishes that we did not merely drift into isolation but dismantled, institution by institution, the structures that carried community, and that the recovery of ordinary, face-to-face belonging is a genuine and measurable good.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Putnam rightly mourns the lost networks and treats community as a resource, a stock of capital that produces useful returns, which is exactly the reduction that hollows community out. A belonging valued for its returns is abandoned the moment the returns fall, when the brother is difficult and the burden is heavy and there is nothing in it for you. Scripture binds Christians to one another not as an investment but as members of one body, where the eye cannot fire the hand for underperforming. The research rightly names the wreckage of association. The gospel supplies a bond that holds precisely where capital would cut its losses, at the place of cost.

secular.source: The research on confession, secrecy, and disclosure
secular.author: Psychology of self-disclosure and the cost of hidden shame
secular.whatItGetsRight: A substantial body of research finds that secrecy is corrosive, that the burdens we carry hidden grow heavier in the dark, and that disclosing them to a trusted other measurably reduces shame, anxiety, and the physical toll of concealment, while bringing relief and reconnection. This is a striking modern confirmation of what the church practiced for centuries and Bonhoeffer recovered, that sin and shame kept secret in the solitude of the heart fester, and that confession to another human being is a genuine means of healing.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research honors the practice and reaches the edge of its deepest meaning without crossing it. It can show that speaking a secret aloud relieves the one who carries it, and it cannot offer what the relief is finally for, the forgiveness that no listener can grant. Disclosure to a therapist eases the weight of shame and cannot lift the guilt of sin, which is owed to God and only pardoned by him. Scripture says confess to one another and be healed, but the healing runs through the cross, the brother hearing the confession as a witness to a mercy he did not buy. The science rightly recovers the power of bringing sin into the light. The gospel names the blood that meets it there.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who equally believe the faith is communal still differ on how thick and how binding the shared life should be, and each emphasis guards against a real failure it has watched happen. The dividing question is whether the recovery of community calls us toward intense, committed, all-of-life common life, or toward a sustainable, ordinary, parish-shaped togetherness that an everyday family can keep for decades. Hear each view at its strongest, because the wisest practitioners borrow from both and the difference is mostly one of intensity and pace.

views.view: The thick community: share life all the way down
views.body: This view holds that the recovery of the body requires going much further than the modern church dares, toward a committed, intense, all-of-life community that touches schedules, homes, finances, and the daily texture of ordinary days. It takes seriously that the Acts church held things in common, that Bonhoeffer and the monastics built shared life with real structure and vows, and that the thin Sunday-attendance Christianity of the West is precisely the watered-down version that forms no one. So it presses toward households that live near each other, eat together often, open their finances, confess their sins, and bind themselves to a particular people they have promised not to abandon when the friction comes. Advocates argue that the one-anothers simply cannot be obeyed at the depth Scripture intends inside the polite, distant, scheduled relationships most churches settle for, that real burden-bearing and real confession require a closeness the modern Christian flees, and that only a community thick enough to be inconvenient can actually form a disciple. The failure they are guarding against is real, a church of acquaintances who share a parking lot and nothing else, where the one-anothers are preached and never practiced because no one is close enough to obey them. They are quick to add that thick community must keep Bonhoeffer's warning in view, that the wish-dream of the perfect intense community destroys the actual people God gives, and that intensity pursued as an ideal becomes its own idol.

views.view: The ordinary parish: build togetherness that lasts
views.body: This view holds that the recovery of the body is best pursued through committed, ordinary, sustainable togetherness, the long faithfulness of an everyday family rooted in a particular congregation and neighborhood over decades. It takes seriously that most believers are called to ordinary lives with jobs and children and limits, that the intense experiments in radical community have a long history of burning bright and burning out, and that Bonhoeffer himself warned against loving the dream of community more than the people in front of you. So it presses toward staying put, joining one church and not leaving, knowing the actual neighbors, keeping the ordinary rhythms of shared meals and mutual care and confession at a pace a tired family can sustain for a lifetime. Advocates argue that the one-anothers are obeyed best not in a heroic season of intensity but in the unglamorous faithfulness of showing up for the same people year after year, and that a community built to be sustainable will still be bearing burdens long after the intense one has exhausted itself. The failure they are guarding against is real, the burnout and the spiritual pride and the eventual collapse of communities that demanded more than ordinary people could give and mistook intensity for holiness. They are quick to add that ordinary must never curdle into the comfortable distance it was reacting against, that a parish faith which never costs anything and never gets close enough to chafe has quietly become the very privatized Christianity it meant to escape.

parts.title: What the Body Forms in the One Who Stays
parts.body:
Community does not only meet your needs. It forms you, and this is the part the lonely consumer of religion never discovers, because the formation only begins once you stay long enough to be inconvenienced. The moment you bind yourself to a real body of real people, God begins to use the friction of their nearness to make you into someone you could never have become alone.

It forms the death of the wish-dream, which is the first and hardest gift. You arrive with a fantasy of community, a picture of the warm, understanding, like-minded people you will finally be known by, and the actual people God gives you are difficult, ordinary, and not what you ordered. Bonhoeffer saw that this disappointment is not the failure of community but the beginning of it, the necessary death of an idol you were worshiping in community's name. When the dream dies, you stop loving your idea of these people and start loving the people, and only then does anything real become possible. The body forms you by disappointing you, and the disappointment is grace.

It forms the patience and forgiveness that no solitary life ever requires. You cannot learn to bear with people in a room by yourself, and the body puts you among people you must bear with, the one who talks too long, the one who failed you, the one whose politics or temperament grate, and it sands away the smooth self-image you maintained so easily in isolation. You discover, in the friction, how impatient and unforgiving and self-protective you actually are, and that discovery is not the community failing you. It is the workshop of sanctification doing precisely what an empty room never could, showing you your sin so the Spirit can kill it.

And it forms a person increasingly unable to imagine the faith without the others, until the private Christianity you once thought was maturity looks like the poverty it always was. As you confess your sins to a brother and feel the weight lift, as you carry a burden too heavy for one person and watch the body absorb it, as you are loved on a day you were unlovable by people who knew you and stayed, you are slowly remade into a member, a hand that has remembered it belongs to a body and would no more leave it than a hand would saw itself off. That is the deepest thing common life forms in you, the unlearning of the lie that you were ever meant to do this alone, and the slow homecoming into the people God saved you to belong to, a foretaste, in a flawed room full of difficult saints, of the city where you will be known fully and loved completely and never, ever again be alone.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: A communal faith is not recovered by admiring the idea of one. It is recovered by leaving the back row, binding yourself to a particular people, and beginning to actually do the one-anothers, which can only ever be done to an other in front of you. None of what follows requires a perfect church or unusual gifts. All of it requires the willingness to be known, to be inconvenienced, and to stay. Begin this week, with one step out of your isolation.

steps: Name your own isolation honestly before God, and confess it as the wound it is rather than the maturity you called it. Ask the Lord to show you where you have built a private faith he never authorized, and to give you the courage to be known by a real people.

Move out of the back row this Sunday. Stay after the service, learn one person's name and one true thing about their week, and let yourself be slightly inconvenienced. The body cannot form a person who arrives late, sits anonymously, and leaves before the benediction.

Reach out to one Christian and ask to meet, simply to know and be known, with no agenda but presence. Most believers are as lonely as you and waiting for someone to take the first step, and the recovery of community begins with one ordinary invitation.

Do one concrete one-another this week. Carry a burden, send the encouraging word, show up with a meal, sit with someone in their trouble. The one-anothers are not concepts to admire but actions to perform, and a single obeyed command teaches more than a year of agreeing with the idea.

Commit to one local church as a member and not a consumer, and stop shopping. The single most important decision in recovering a communal faith is to bind yourself to a particular flawed people you have promised not to abandon, because you are only formed by the body you cannot leave.

Join or start a small group where actual life is shared, not merely a study attended. Find the few people with whom you will go beneath the small talk, and protect a regular night together the way you protect a bill that must be paid, because depth is the fruit of repetition over time.

Begin to be honest about your real life with one trusted believer. Bring something out of the dark, a struggle, a fear, a sin you have hidden, and let the relief of being known begin to teach you why the New Testament commands confession to one another. What you keep secret festers, and what you confess can be healed.

Let the death of the wish-dream begin when these people disappoint you, as they will. When the group is awkward or the church frustrates you or someone fails you, resist the urge to flee to an imagined better community, and stay, because Bonhoeffer was right that the dying of the dream is the door to the real thing.

Build burden-bearing into your community on purpose, so that the one-anothers become a rhythm and not an accident. Make it normal to ask how is it actually with your soul, to know one another's troubles by name, and to show up in the hard seasons with presence and casseroles and prayer. A body that shares burdens is doing the most ordinary and most radical thing in the world.

Open your home and your table to your church family and your neighbors, weaving the communal life into the place you live. Common faith is not sustained in a building one hour a week but in the homes and meals and shared ordinary days where the early church actually lived, so let your door begin to stand open.

Recover confession as a regular practice with someone trustworthy, dragging your hidden sins into the light where Christ can kill them. The Protestant church largely lost this and is the poorer for it, and the brother who hears your confession becomes a living witness that the mercy of God is real and meant for you.

Practice forgiveness as the friction comes, because in a real body it will. When you are wronged, do the hard and concrete work of forgiving as you have been forgiven, refusing both the false peace of pretending and the slow poison of resentment. The one-anothers include forgive one another, and a community that cannot forgive will not survive its first real wound.

Settle into the long faithfulness of staying with one people through the seasons when community is sweet and the seasons when it costs, trusting that you are formed by those you do not leave. The deepest fruit of the body comes not in the intense early months but in the unglamorous decade of showing up for the same flawed saints.

Move from being served by the community to building it, taking responsibility for the belonging of others as you have received it. Watch for the lonely newcomer, the back-row visitor, the isolated believer, and do for them what someone did for you, because a Christian who only consumes community has not yet understood the body.

Order your whole life toward the people God has given you rather than fitting them into the margins. Let where you live, how you spend, and how you keep your calendar be shaped by the body you belong to, because a communal faith that never touches your schedule, your money, or your address is still the private faith wearing a friendlier face.

Keep the common life pointed at the city it is preparing you for, through every disappointment and every reconciliation and every burden shared. Build your life together, in a flawed room full of difficult and beloved saints, as a small and stubborn outpost of the great gathering at the end of all things, the countless multitude where the body is whole and the loneliness is over and the God who is himself a communion welcomes his people, at last, fully home.
